title: Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change — Chapter 12: Cross-Sectoral Perspectives (Carbon Dioxide Removal)
principal: the authors of Climate Change 2022: Mitigation of Climate Change — Chapter 12: Cross-Sectoral Perspectives (Carbon Dioxide Removal)

objections.claim_quoted: Carbon dioxide removal (CDR) is assessed as a necessary element to achieve net zero CO2 and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions both globally and nationally, because it counterbalances residual emissions from hard-to-transition sectors (robust evidence, high agreement) [1].
objections.objection: The page gives CDR's necessity without the chapter's paired statement that CDR does not replace deep emission cuts, which limits what 'necessary' implies.
objections.source_says: To avoid CDR being misperceived as a substitute for deep emissions reductions, the prioritisation of emissions cuts can be signalled and achieved with differentiated target setting for reductions and removals
objections.locator: Passage on target setting for CDR and emissions reductions (Geden et al. 2019; McLaren et al. 2019)
objections.could_not_find: I did not retrieve the verbatim Cross-Chapter Box 8 sentence. This wording comes from the factsheet.
objections.why: The page's conclusion that CDR is necessary stands. A reader could take 'necessary' as licence to lean on removals, and the chapter limits CDR to residual emissions plus later net-negative phases.
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="19-1">"CDR is not a substitute for deep emissions reductions"</cite>. This is from the IPCC WGIII CDR Factsheet, which summarises Ch. 12 / Cross-Chapter Box 8, not from the chapter text itself.

objections.claim_quoted: Some methods have been practised for decades to millennia, though not necessarily to remove carbon, including afforestation, improved forest management, wetland restoration and soil carbon sequestration [1].
objections.objection: The page contrasts established with novel methods on maturity alone and omits the chapter's trade-off: vegetation, soil and sediment methods are cheaper and easier but store carbon for less time and are more vulnerable.
objections.source_says: carbon stored in vegetation or through SCS has shorter storage times and is more vulnerable than carbon stored in buildings as wood products
objections.locator: Second excerpt, sentence beginning 'Furthermore, carbon stored in vegetation or through SCS...'
objections.could_not_find: I did not retrieve the verbatim 12.3 / Table 12.6 text on durability and vulnerability. This comes from the factsheet summary. The chapter's own wording and its table of storage timescales should be checked.
objections.why: A page that lists the old methods only as 'practised for decades' implies they are the mature, safe side. The chapter says their lower cost and co-benefits come with less durable storage.
objections.source_says_first: Paraphrase, not a verbatim chapter quote: per the WGIII CDR Factsheet, <cite index="19-8">options based on storage in vegetation, soils or sediments are easier and cheaper and have biodiversity or food-security co-benefits, but hold carbon for less time and are more vulnerable</cite>. The factsheet also says <cite index="19-5">inappropriate large-scale deployment can increase competition for land</cite>.

objections.claim_quoted: Studies have shown that the life-cycle net emissions of DACCS systems can be negative, even with some current energy mixes, with the GHG intensity of the energy used being a key factor [1].
objections.objection: The page gives only the favourable side of the energy-mix finding and omits the chapter's figure showing that grid emissions can substantially cut net removal.
objections.source_says: The emissions associated with this additional energy generation may reduce the net carbon dioxide removal by up to 30% with present-day grid average emissions, but this efficiency loss would decrease with low-carbon power ( Beerling et al. 2020 ).
objections.locator: Section 12.3 (Enhanced weathering discussion of energy requirements and net CDR)
objections.could_not_find: The retrieved text is a fragment. I could not confirm which methods the 30% applies to (BECCS, DACCS or both), or the full caption. Please check Figure 12.3 before acting on this.
objections.why: 'Can be negative' is true but is the lenient reading. If the 30% figure applies to the methods the page discusses, the quantified penalty from present-day energy should sit next to it.
objections.source_says_first: Figure 12.3 caption (truncated in the version I retrieved): <cite index="1-6">"may reduce the net carbon dioxide removal by up to 30% with present day grid"</cite>.

objections.claim_quoted: Because residual non-CO2 emissions are expected to be significant, the gap between the two could reach one to several decades [1].
objections.objection: 'The two' has no antecedent. The sentence the chapter places immediately before it, that net zero CO2 comes earlier than net zero GHG, is missing, so the reader cannot tell what the gap is between.
objections.source_says: Net zero CO 2 emissions will be achieved earlier than net zero GHG emissions. As volumes of residual non-CO 2 emissions are expected to be significant, this time-lag could reach one to several decades, depending on the respective size and composition of residual GHG emissions at the time of net zero CO 2 emissions.
objections.locator: Cross-Chapter Box 8 (Chapter 12), paragraph beginning '2021 ), achieving net zero GHG implies gross CO 2 removals...'
objections.why: This is a presentation fault. As written, the 'decades' claim cannot be interpreted. The page's later net-negative sentences depend on the CO2-before-GHG ordering.
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="5-1">"Net zero CO 2 emissions will be achieved earlier than net zero GHG emissions."</cite> Section 12.3 / Cross-Chapter Box 8 then ties the gap to the size and composition of residual emissions.

title: Climate Change 2023: Synthesis Report (AR6 SYR)
principal: the authors of Climate Change 2023: Synthesis Report (AR6 SYR)

objections.claim_quoted: As a result, net zero CO2 is reached earlier than net zero GHGs (high confidence) [2].
objections.objection: The page attaches this gap to hard-to-abate residual emissions needing CDR, but the Synthesis Report ties it to residual non-CO2 emissions (CH4, N2O, F-gases) that remain when net zero CO2 is reached.
objections.source_says: While non-CO2 GHG emissions are strongly reduced in all pathways that limit warming to 2°C (>67%) or lower, residual emissions of CH4 and N2O and F-gases of about 8 [5–11] GtCO2-eq yr-1 remain at the time of
objections.locator: Section 3 (Section 3.3.3 text on net zero timing), passage following 'Global net zero CO2 emissions are reached in the early 2050s...'; the sentence is cut off in the held text by footnote text
objections.why: The page's 'as a result' makes the gap look like a consequence of the sectors it just listed. The report puts the non-CO2 residual of about 8 GtCO2-eq per year at the centre of the explanation, and that is the figure that sizes the CDR needed for net zero GHG.
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="2-6">"residual emissions of CH4 and N2O and F-gases of about 8 [5–11] GtCO2-eq yr-1 remain"</cite>. The sentence begins by saying non-CO2 GHGs are strongly reduced in all pathways limiting warming to 2°C (>67%) or lower. It is cut off in the retrieved text, so I could not confirm exactly what the residuals remain at.

objections.claim_quoted: CDR will be necessary to achieve net negative CO2 emissions [2].
objections.objection: The page says CDR is necessary and leaves out the report's finding that the methods now in use are almost entirely conventional land-based ones, which bears on how far CDR can be scaled.
objections.source_says: Afforestation, reforestation, improved forest management, agroforestry and soil carbon sequestration are currently the only widely practiced CDR methods (high confidence).
objections.locator: Held text, CDR section: the passage following 'Estimated storage timescales vary from decades to centuries...'
objections.why: 'Necessary' stands, but the page reads as if CDR is an established tool. The same omission affects the 'unavoidable' sentence that opens the page's CDR passage, 'It does not replace cutting emissions…'. The report adds that CDR methods differ in maturity, cost and risk, and that deployment levels in modelled pathways depend on assumptions about costs, availability and constraints (high confidence).
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="33-5">"currently the only widely practiced CDR methods"</cite> is the report's wording for afforestation, reforestation, improved forest management, agroforestry and soil carbon sequestration. The report gives this finding high confidence.

objections.claim_quoted: achieving and sustaining net negative global CO2 emissions, with annual rates of CDR greater than residual CO2 emissions, would gradually reduce the warming level again (high confidence)
objections.objection: The page says net negative emissions would reduce warming and omits the report's quantification of how much removal that takes.
objections.source_says: Reducing global temperature by removing CO2 would require net negative emissions of 220 GtCO2 (best estimate, with a likely range of 160 to 370 GtCO2) for every tenth of a degree (medium confidence).
objections.locator: Section 3 (Long-term Climate Change), paragraph following the remaining carbon budget discussion
objections.why: 'Gradually reduce' reads as cheap and open-ended. The report says each 0.1°C of reversal needs about 220 GtCO2 of net removal, which is a large share of the 500 GtCO2 remaining carbon budget for 1.5°C. That scale is what makes the feasibility concern concrete.
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="29-5">"net negative emissions of 220 GtCO2 (best estimate, with a likely range of 160 to 370 GtCO2) for every tenth of a degree (medium confidence)"</cite>

objections.claim_quoted: the larger the overshoot, the more net negative CO2 emissions would be needed to return to 1.5°C by 2100
objections.objection: The sentence states the direction of the relationship and omits the report's number for it.
objections.source_says: Reducing global temperature by removing CO2 would require net negative emissions of 220 GtCO2 (best estimate, with a likely range of 160 to 370 GtCO2) for every tenth of a degree (medium confidence).
objections.locator: Section 3.3.2 Net Zero Emissions: Timing and Implications (paragraph on net negative emissions and overshoot)
objections.why: The 'faster transition reduces CDR requirement' point is stronger with the report's own figures: 220 GtCO2 for limited overshoot against 360 GtCO2 after high overshoot.
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="30-11">"Reducing global temperature by removing CO2 would require net negative emissions of 220 GtCO2"</cite> per tenth of a degree. The sentence continues with a best estimate and likely range (160–370 GtCO2) and a medium-confidence label. The report also gives median cumulative net negative emissions of 220 GtCO2 by 2100 for limited overshoot and 360 GtCO2 after high overshoot (high confidence).

objections.claim_quoted: According to the IPCC (SR1.5 Summary for Policymakers, B.7.3), the larger the overshoot, the more net negative CO2 emissions would be needed
objections.objection: The page credits this finding to the SR1.5 SPM, but it is a finding of the AR6 Synthesis Report (the page's own source [2]), and SR1.5 has no section B.7.3.
objections.source_says: Modelled pathways that limit warming to 1.5°C (>50%) with no or limited overshoot reach median values of cumulative net negative emissions of 220 GtCO2 by 2100, pathways that return warming to 1.5°C (>50%) after high overshoot reach median values of 360 GtCO2 (high confidence).
objections.locator: AR6 SYR Longer Report, Section 3.3 Mitigation Pathways (net negative emissions paragraph, with footnote 137)
objections.could_not_find: I did not find a passage of the SR1.5 SPM numbered B.7.3 in the retrieved material. SR1.5 is cited in the SYR only as a supporting reference, for example SR1.5 SPM C.1.3 on carbon budgets.
objections.why: This is an attribution error. The finding is real, but a reader who checks SR1.5 B.7.3 will not find it.
objections.source_says_first: The Synthesis Report says that more rapid reductions in CO2 and non-CO2 emissions, particularly methane, reduce the net negative emissions requirement, <cite index="9-9">"thereby reducing feasibility and sustainability concerns, and social and environmental risks"</cite>. This appears in the AR6 SYR overshoot passages. I could not retrieve the exact paragraph number, so I do not assert 'B.7.3' for the SYR.

objections.claim_quoted: Most countries report anthropogenic land CO2 fluxes, including those caused by human-driven environmental change such as CO2 fertilisation, on 'managed' land in their national greenhouse gas inventories [2].
objections.objection: The page quotes the accounting point and drops the sentence that follows it, which states the consequence for budgets, and then calls the passage immaterial.
objections.source_says: Using emissions estimates based on these inventories, the remaining carbon budgets must be correspondingly reduced.
objections.locator: SPM B.5.2, footnote 40 (also the matching footnote to Section 3.3.1 Remaining Carbon Budgets)
objections.why: The inventory sentence on its own has no stated consequence. The report says the consequence is a smaller budget, which bears on net-zero timing and on how much removal is counted. Reporting the consequence while excluding it as 'not material' is inconsistent.
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="22-7">"the remaining carbon budgets must be correspondingly reduced"</cite> when emissions estimates are based on these inventories. The retrieved text places this in footnote 40 to the carbon budget statement, under Section 3.3.1. The retrieved text is silent on the size of the reduction.

objections.claim_quoted: estimates of future CO2 emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure without additional abatement already exceed the remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.5°C (50%) (high confidence)
objections.objection: The page gives no value for the budget and does not say the report's budget is itself conditional on non-CO2 mitigation.
objections.source_says: remaining carbon budgets could be 300 or 600 GtCO2 for 1.5°C (50%), respectively for high and low non-CO2 emissions
objections.locator: SPM footnote 41 to B.5.2 (Summary for Policymakers)
objections.why: The infrastructure finding stands, with high confidence in the report. The page gives the comparison without the budget it is compared to. The same applies to the page's earlier sentence 'projected CO2 emissions from existing fossil fuel infrastructure… would exceed the remaining carbon budget for 1.5°C (50%) (high confidence)'.
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="24-5">"remaining carbon budgets could be 300 or 600 GtCO2 for 1.5°C (50%), respectively for high and low non-CO2 emissions"</cite>. The report's best estimate from the start of 2020 is 500 GtCO2 for 1.5°C (50%) and 1150 GtCO2 for 2°C (67%).

title: Global Warming of 1.5°C — Special Report (SR15)
principal: the authors of Global Warming of 1.5°C — Special Report (SR15)

objections.claim_quoted: In 1.5°C pathways, CDR would be used to compensate for residual emissions and, in most cases, to achieve net negative emissions that return warming to 1.5°C after a peak (high confidence) [3].
objections.objection: The page quotes the sentence that follows the headline finding of SPM C.3 but leaves out the headline itself. That finding is that every 1.5°C pathway with no or limited overshoot uses CDR, and it gives the quantity.
objections.source_says: All pathways that limit global warming to 1.5°C with limited or no overshoot project the use of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) on the order of 100–1000 GtCO 2 over the 21st century.
objections.locator: SPM C.3 (held text: "C.3. All pathways that limit global warming to 1.5°C with limited or no overshoot project the use of carbon dioxide removal (CDR)...")
objections.why: The submission's stated purpose for this source is the claim that all 1.5°C pathways require 100–1000 GtCO2 of CDR. None of the twelve sentences gives that range or says 'all pathways', so a reader cannot see the scale or universality of the CDR requirement. The other sentences, such as 'a few hundred GtCO2' and 'several hundreds of GtCO2', cannot be placed against it.
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="2-4">All pathways that limit global warming to 1.5°C with limited or no overshoot project the use of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) on the order of 100–1000 GtCO2 over the 21st century.</cite> (SPM C.3, first sentence)

objections.claim_quoted: Significant near-term emissions reductions, together with measures to lower energy and land demand, can limit CDR deployment to a few hundred GtCO2 without reliance on bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) (high confidence) [3].
objections.objection: Without the 100–1000 GtCO2 range, 'a few hundred GtCO2' reads as an escape from CDR. In the SPM it is a lower-end case within a range that still requires CDR in every 1.5°C pathway.
objections.source_says: All pathways that limit global warming to 1.5°C with limited or no overshoot project the use of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) on the order of 100–1000 GtCO 2 over the 21st century.
objections.why: The page presents the 'few hundred GtCO2' limit as a mitigation lever. It never says that CDR remains in all 1.5°C pathways, even at the low end. Anyone who reads the page's sentences without the range could think low CDR use means no CDR.
objections.source_says_first: <cite index="2-4">on the order of 100–1000 GtCO2 over the 21st century</cite> is projected in all 1.5°C pathways with limited or no overshoot (SPM C.3). The 'few hundred GtCO2' case sits inside that range and still includes CDR.

objections.claim_quoted: Effective governance is needed to limit such trade-offs and to ensure that carbon removals are permanent (high confidence) [3].
objections.objection: The page lists constraints on CDR but omits the SPM's finding on how feasibility and sustainability could be improved: a portfolio of options at lesser scale. This is the SPM's answer to the constraints the page lists.
objections.source_says: Feasibility and sustainability of CDR use could be enhanced by a portfolio of options deployed at substantial, but lesser scales, rather than a single option at very large scale ( high confidence ).
objections.locator: SPM section C.3.4 (the passage following C.3.3 on CDR and overshoot)
objections.why: The page shows only the constraints and trade-offs of CDR. The SPM also says a portfolio at lesser scale could ease them, so leaving this out makes the feasibility picture more one-sided than the source.
objections.source_says_first: From memory, not verified verbatim in the retrieved text: "Feasibility and sustainability of CDR use could be enhanced by a portfolio of options deployed at substantial, but lesser scale than in many 1.5°C pathways (limited evidence, high agreement)." A partial fragment appears in the SPM text as <cite index="3-5">by a portfolio of options deployed at substantial, but lesser scales</cite>.

objections.claim_quoted: Afforestation and bioenergy may compete with other land uses (high confidence) [3].
objections.objection: The SPM sentence goes on to name the affected systems. The page cuts it off after land competition.
objections.source_says: Afforestation and bioenergy may compete with other land uses and may have significant impacts on agricultural and food systems, biodiversity, and other ecosystem functions and services ( high confidence ).
objections.could_not_find: The retrieved search excerpts did not reproduce this sentence in full. I am relying on recall of SPM C.3 and have not confirmed the exact wording.
objections.why: The omission understates the SPM's stated impacts of land-based CDR on food, biodiversity and ecosystems. The page's conclusion on feasibility constraints still stands.
objections.source_says_first: From memory, not verified verbatim in the retrieved text: afforestation and bioenergy "may compete with other land uses and may have significant impacts on agricultural and food systems, biodiversity, and other ecosystem functions and services (high confidence)."

title: Negative emissions—Part 1: Research landscape and synthesis
principal: the authors of Negative emissions—Part 1: Research landscape and synthesis

objections.claim_quoted: Soil carbon sinks saturate, and they are reversible if the management practice that promotes them stops [5].
objections.objection: The page quotes only the permanence caveat from the soil-carbon row of the synthesis table and leaves out the rest of that row: its potential, its cost range, and the positive-cost-impact entries.
objections.source_says: SCS n/a n/a n/a n/a 2–5 [0.5–11] 0–100 [−45–100] Improved soil resilience and improved agricultural production; negative cost options; reduced pollution and improved soil quality; positive impacts on soil, water and air quality
objections.locator: Table 3 (Summary of insights on costs, potentials, side-effects...), SCS row
objections.why: The saturation and reversibility caveat is accurate. Quoted alone, though, it reads as a verdict on soil carbon. The same table row presents soil carbon as available now, at large scale, with some negative-cost options, and names permanence as the concern.
objections.source_says_first: Synthesis table, SCS row: potential "2–5 [0.5–11]" and cost "0–100 [−45–100]", with benefits listed as <cite index="15-6">"Improved soil resilience and improved agricultural production; negative cost options"</cite>. The same row marks SCS as "Available at large scale" and lists "Incentives for widespread adoption; concerns about permanence" as the barriers.

objections.claim_quoted: One review notes that available scenarios achieve large-scale removal almost exclusively with BECCS [5].
objections.objection: The page reports BECCS dominance in scenarios but not the review's finding that no single NET, BECCS included, can sustainably deliver that scale, and that a portfolio of NETs at modest scales is the route it points to.
objections.source_says: Third, any single NET is unlikely to sustainably achieve the large NETs deployment observed in many 1.5 ◦ C and 2 ◦ C mitigation scenarios. Yet, portfolios of multiple NETs, each deployed at modest scales, could be invaluable for reaching the climate goals.
objections.locator: Opening summary of major findings (third of six findings)
objections.why: The BECCS dominance sentence is accurate. By itself it implies that removal rests on one technology. The review's own answer is that scenario reliance on BECCS is a feature of the scenarios, and that a portfolio is the alternative.
objections.source_says_first: Abstract: <cite index="5-6,5-7">"any single NET is unlikely to sustainably achieve the large NETs deployment observed in many 1.5 °C and 2 °C mitigation scenarios. Yet, portfolios of multiple NETs, each deployed at modest scales, could be invaluable for reaching the climate goals."</cite> Abstract: <cite index="5-1">"accounting for economic and biophysical limits, we identify relevant potentials for all NETs except ocean fertilization."</cite>

objections.claim_quoted: The same review reports great scepticism that modelled removals of 10–20 GtCO2 per year late this century can be achieved by BECCS alone or by any other single method [5].
objections.objection: The page gives the scepticism about single-technology scale-up but omits the review's stated conclusion that follows from it: modest-scale portfolios of several NETs are valuable, and potentials exist for all NETs except ocean fertilization.
objections.source_says: Yet, portfolios of multiple NETs, each deployed at modest scales, could be invaluable for reaching the climate goals.
objections.locator: Abstract, sixth-finding list (third finding, following 'any single NET is unlikely to sustainably achieve the large NETs deployment')
objections.why: A reader of the page's sentence would conclude that large-scale removal is doubtful in general. The review's conclusion is narrower: no single NET delivers it, and portfolios at modest scales are still worth having. The page uses the doubt and omits the review's answer to it.
objections.source_says_first: Abstract: <cite index="5-7">"Yet, portfolios of multiple NETs, each deployed at modest scales, could be invaluable for reaching the climate goals."</cite> Abstract, second finding: <cite index="5-1">"accounting for economic and biophysical limits, we identify relevant potentials for all NETs except ocean fertilization."</cite> The scepticism sentence itself sits in the synthesis section and cites Anderson and Peters 2016, Anderson 2015 and Geden 2015, which are technology-literature sources.

objections.claim_quoted: It also finds that adding negative emission technologies to cost-optimising scenarios reduces long-term mitigation costs but impedes early emissions reductions [5].
objections.objection: The page omits what the review says immediately after this finding: the early-reduction shortfall is a budget overshoot that is paid back later through net negative emissions, and the review quantifies the near-term gap when CCS-based removal is not allowed.
objections.source_says: The resulting budget overshoot is ‘paid back’ towards the end of the century during a sustained period of net negative emissions, i.e. a global net removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
objections.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The introduction of NETs in cost-optimizing mitigation scenarios reduces the costs of long-term mitigation but impedes early emissions reductions (see also figure 8).'
objections.why: The review presents the delay as the mechanism of a cost-optimising overshoot-and-repay trade-off, and it ties near-term dependence on NETs to the pace of near-term cuts. Without that, the sentence reads as a bare cost of NETs. The review's concern is that the repayment depends on removals being delivered at scale later, which links back to the scepticism in the previous sentence.
objections.source_says_first: Same passage: <cite index="11-1,11-2">"The resulting budget overshoot is 'paid back' towards the end of the century during a sustained period"</cite> of net negative emissions. Figure 8: <cite index="20-6">"near-term CO2 reductions are typically far steeper—in this example reaching a 9.1 GtCO2 gap by 2030."</cite> Also, <cite index="20-7">"If near-term emission reductions follow the pathways suggested by current NDCs there will be a fundamental dependence on negative emissions by 2030 in 2 °C scenarios."</cite>
